title: W10: Null Hypothesis Significance Testing (NHST)
text:
Pick someone new to be the driver this week. If everyone in the group has already had a week as the driver, start going round again!
The driver will type the code. The rest of you are navigators, you need to tell the driver where to go (i.e., what to type!).
Driver instructions:

Log in to the bigger screen at your table
Open RStudio Server
Open a new .R script, and load the tidyverse package.
Listen to your navigators

Navigator instructions:

Tell your driver where to go (i.e., what to type)!


TODO CHECK UN - are you okay with all of this being called Z even though it should technically be t? the idea being that the explanation (at least a very brief one) comes next week TODO CHECK UN - would you prefer this is two-sided?

Question 1


This week, we’re going to draw on the ideas we covered over the last few weeks and go step-by-step through the process of performing a ‘null hypothesis significance test’.
We start with a research question:

Research Question: Are first year undergraduate students more optimistic than adults in general?
Operationalisation: We surveyed students on a first year undergraduate statistics course (that’s you!), and asked them to indicate their level of pessimism/optimism on a sliding scale from -100 (pessimist) to +100 (optimist). Previous research using this measure suggests that the overall adult population has an average score of 35.
Data: https://uoepsy.github.io/data/dapr1_2526_survey.csv

Task: Define the null and alternative hypotheses.

🗂️ See TODO defining h0 h1? flashcard flash card.






Solution



Solution 1. \(H_0: \mu - 35 = 0\) \(H_1: \mu - 35 > 0\)




Question 2


In future, we’re going to learn and use functions in R that do all the steps of NHST for us, but for this week we’re going to break down the process, so we’re going to need all the different parts.
We’re going to need:

the size of our sample
the mean that we observe in our sample
the hypothesised value that we are testing if our sample mean is equal to
(an estimate of) how much we expect samples of our size to vary

Write down or calculate each of these now.






TipHints





for d., this is the “standard error”. We have seen the formula for this a few times, it’s \(\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\). As this is real research, we don’t know \(\sigma\) (the standard deviation of scores in the population), so we’ll estimate it using \(s\), the standard deviation in our sample.








Solution



Solution 2. 

library(tidyverse)
sdata <- read_csv("https://uoepsy.github.io/data/dapr1_2526_survey.csv")

nrow(sdata)

[1] 41

mean(sdata$outlook)

[1] 42.7

35

[1] 35

sd(sdata$outlook) / sqrt(nrow(sdata))

[1] 4.12






Question 3


Together, the information from the previous question allow us to build up a picture of “what would sample means be like if the null hypothesis (\(H_0\)) were true”.
We can then calculate the probability of seeing a sample mean at least as extreme as the one we have seen, if the null hypothesis were true:








Figure 1: Null hypothesis testing in a nutshell. SE stands for ‘standard error’.





To calculate the probability areas, we’re going to need to get convert our mean into a “test statistic”.
This is called a “Z-statistic”, and it bears a similar resemblance to what we did a few weeks back in calculating “Z-scores”. In this case, however, we are doing the process on the weird abstract theoretical distribution of “the means from all the possible samples we could have taken”.
\[
Z = \frac{M - \mu_0}{SE}
\]
Task: Calculate Z





Solution



Solution 3. 

zstat <- 
  ( mean(sdata$outlook) - 35 ) / 
    ( sd(sdata$outlook) / sqrt(nrow(sdata)) )

zstat

[1] 1.87






Question 4


Now that we have our test statistic, we can calculate the “p-value”.
This is “probability of seeing a sample mean at least as extreme as the one we have seen, if the null hypothesis were true”, and corresponds to one, or both, of the shaded red areas in Figure 1, depending on how we phrased \(H_1\).
Z statistics are normally distributed with a mean of 0 and standard deviation of 1, so we just need to use pnorm() to find the area of the normal distribution curve that is beyond our Z statistic.






TipHint





think i need a hint here about direction








Solution



Solution 4. Area greater:

1-pnorm(zstat)

[1] 0.0311

Question 1


We’re continuing to use the same dataset for the next couple of weeks (the survey that many of you completed in the first week). The data are stored at https://uoepsy.github.io/data/dapr1_2526_survey.csv (Check back to your work from the previous weeks to remind yourself how to get the data into R).
Calculate the Inter Quartile Range (IQR) for:

distance_born - the distances from Edinburgh that the respondents were born. The IQR is appropriate here because the variable is highly skewed.

spicy_num - the levels of spice that respondents like. The IQR is appropriate here because the variable is ordinal.


🗂️ See Measure variability > IQR flash card.






Solution



Solution 1. 

library(tidyverse)
sdata <- read_csv("https://uoepsy.github.io/data/dapr1_2526_survey.csv")

sdata |> 
  summarise(
    dist_IQR = IQR(distance_born, na.rm = TRUE),
    spice_IQR = IQR(spicy_num, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# A tibble: 1 x 2
  dist_IQR spice_IQR
     <dbl>     <dbl>
1    1265.         0






Question 2


The survey also asked people to rate, on scales of 0 to 100, three things:







variable
question




sleepqual
“how well do you tend to sleep on average?”


procrast
“how often do you tend to procrastinate on tasks or responsibilities on average?”


multitask
“how well do you think you can handle multiple tasks or responsibilities at the same time on average?”



Calculate the mean and standard deviation for one of these variables.

🗂️ See Measure variability > SD flash card.






Solution



Solution 2. 

sdata |> 
  summarise(
    sleep_M = mean(sleepqual, na.rm = TRUE),
    sleep_SD = sd(sleepqual, na.rm = TRUE),
    procr_M = mean(procrast, na.rm = TRUE),
    procr_SD = sd(procrast, na.rm = TRUE),
    mutli_M = mean(multitask, na.rm = TRUE),
    multi_SD = sd(multitask, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# A tibble: 1 x 6
  sleep_M sleep_SD procr_M procr_SD mutli_M multi_SD
    <dbl>    <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>
1    70.9     10.5    29.5     5.01      40     12.4






Question 3


For the sleep-quality, procrastination, and multitasking variables, respondents were given the scale from 0 to 100. That doesn’t necessarily mean that people used the whole scale.
For the same variable you chose in the previous question, calculate its range.

🗂️ See Measure variability > Range flash card.






Solution



Solution 3. We’ve provided below the range of all 3 variables, so you can check your answer whichever one you chose.

sdata |> 
  summarise(
    sleep_R = max(sleepqual, na.rm = TRUE) - min(sleepqual, na.rm = TRUE),
    procr_R = max(procrast, na.rm = TRUE) - min(procrast, na.rm = TRUE),
    multi_R = max(multitask, na.rm = TRUE) - min(multitask, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# A tibble: 1 x 3
  sleep_R procr_R multi_R
    <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>
1      45      21      51






Question 4


In one call to summarise() (that is, using the function only once), calculate descriptive statistics of central tendency and variability for all three variables sleepqual, procrast and multitask.





Solution



Solution 4. 

sdata |> 
  summarise(
    sleep_m = mean(sleepqual, na.rm = TRUE),
    sleep_s = sd(sleepqual, na.rm = TRUE),
    procr_m = mean(procrast, na.rm = TRUE),
    procr_s = sd(procrast, na.rm = TRUE),
    multi_m = mean(multitask, na.rm = TRUE),
    multi_s = sd(multitask, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# A tibble: 1 x 6
  sleep_m sleep_s procr_m procr_s multi_m multi_s
    <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>
1    70.9    10.5    29.5    5.01      40    12.4






Question 5


The survey also included questions asking about whether people perceive themselves as pessimists vs optimists (the outlook variable), and as an “evening person” vs a “morning person” (the ampm variable).

Consequently, the central tendency for chronotype is best described by the (7)______ of (8)______ ((9)______), with scores ranging from (10)______ to (11)______.







TipHints

title: W1: Introductions
text:
This week’s workshop is quite minimal. All we’re really wanting you to do is:

Explore the software and start playing around.

Meet some new people, make some new friends, and form a group to work with in these workshops.

From next week, you’ll be working in these groups collaboratively on the workshop questions, with one person doing the typing (the ‘driver’) and the others telling them what to type (the ‘navigators’). The role of driver will swap each week, so you’ll always get a turn at typing.


Question 1


The very first task here is to open RStudio.
R and RStudio is software that you can download and install on your computer, but for the duration of this course, we are providing you with a version on a server.
You can access the RStudio server here: https://rstudio.ppls.ed.ac.uk.
We would recommend you bookmark the page so that you can easily find it again!




Question 2


The first thing to do is start using R just like a calculator.
Try doing some basic calculations by typing in the bottom left where you see the blue > and pressing enter.
Playing with these: *, /, +, -, ^ and seeing what happens - can you work out what each one does?






Tipstuck seeing a + symbol?





If we give R an incomplete request, then it will just stay waiting for it to be finished.
e.g., if we typed a query and missed a bracket, then R would just leave a + symbol to say “I’m waiting for more…”:

To get out of this we can either type the required stuff to finish the query, or, much more simply, just press the Escape key (Esc) on your keyboard and it will cancel the query and let you start it again.







Question 3


In order to save our work, we need to start writing our commands in a document. Something we can edit, save, come back to later on, and share with other people.

Open an R Script (File > New File > R Script).

A new window will pop up in the top left of RStudio. Write some calculations in there (put each one on a new line).

You’ll notice that writing in the script doesn’t actually perform the calculations. We need to “Run” the commands we are writing, which we can do by ensuring the cursor is on the line we want to run, and then either:

press Ctrl+Enter (or Cmd+Enter for Mac)OR
clicking the “Run” button in the top right of the R Script.






Question 4



# starting a line with a "#" turns it into a comment
# it means that R will not try to run it  

# we can store things in R's memory using "name <- value", e.g.:
my_name <- "Umberto"
about_me <- "Italian."
fun_fact <- "I can play the piano."

# this -- paste() -- is a "function". 
# it takes some inputs, and gives us outputs
# in this case, we give it a whole load of separate sentence fragments
# and it sticks them together: 
paste("Hello, my name is", my_name, 
      "and I am", about_me,
      "Fun fact:", fun_fact)


Copy-Paste the lines of code above into your R Script and edit them to provide some text about yourself (if you don’t want to share a fun fact about yourself, just share a random fun fact!)
Save your script (File > Save).
Close your script (there’s a little cross in the tab label at the top of the script)
Re-open your script (File > Open)
Celebrate!





Question 5


Finally, we’d like you to join your group on Blackboard Learn.
Groups are named based on the workshop (1, 2, 3, 4, 5) and your table number.
So if this is Workshop 3, and you are sitting at table 6, you should join group “Group 3_06”.

Go to the course LEARN page
click Groups on the top menu bar.
click Workshops_1_2_3_4_5
Join your group
Now click on “Group Discussion Space” within the Quick Links folder of LEARN.
Upload your script to the discussion space, to share your fun fact with your group members.

Question 4


Go through each variable and write down what type of variable it is (e.g., is it continuous, categorical, or ordinal?)






TipHints





Revisit the slides about different data types.








Solution



Solution 4. 

Name is categorical nominal, and it is the identifier variable.
Birthday month is categorical ordinal.
Number of siblings is continuous (discrete).
Spicy food preference is categorical ordinal.
Eye colour is categorical nominal.
Distance between Edinburgh and birthplace is numerical (continuous).
Optimism scale is numerical (continuous).
Morningness scale is categorical (ordinal).
Sleep quality is categorical (ordinal).
Multi-taskin scale is categorical (ordinal).
Favourite colour is categorical (nominal).
Preferred pet is categorical (nominal).
Description of self is categorical (nominal).





Question 5


R will by default treat a variable with only numbers in it as a numeric variable, and anything else as a “character” variable (“character” = any letters/numbers/symbols).
Change the eye_colour variable to a factor in R, that only has the options “brown”, “blue”, “green” or “hazel”.

🗂️ See Mutate columns and Manage factor variables flash cards.

What happens when you now do skim(data)? How does it treat this variable differently?






TipHints





Here is the basic code structure for taking a dataframe named mydata and adding a new variable (or changing an existing one).

Line 2 takes the data, and passes it to line 3.

Lines 3-5 “mutates” the data, adding a variable called new_variable. The new_variable is going to contain the values of an existing variable (old_variable) but with some function applied to them. For example, if we had new_variable = old_variable/2 then it would contain the same values but halved.
It feels odd, but it helps to think about the first line of code once we’ve thought of the others. This line re-assigns the name mydata to the mutated mydata, thereby making the change save to the object in R’s memory.


mydata <-
  mydata |> 
  mutate(
    new_variable = function(old_variable)
  )

To make a variable a factor, the function we want is factor(). This will consider every different value that we have to be a possible category:

factor(variable)

If we want to have a specific set of possible values, we can do so with the levels part of the function, replacing the "..." with the options we consider valid:

factor(variable, levels = c("...","...","...", ....... ))











Solution



Solution 5. 

sdata <-
  sdata |>
  mutate(
    eye_colour = factor(eye_colour, levels = c("brown","blue","green","hazel"))
  )

Question 1


We’re continuing to use the same dataset for the next couple of weeks (the survey that many of you completed in the first week). The data are stored at https://uoepsy.github.io/data/dapr1_2526_survey.csv (Check back to your work from the previous two weeks to remind yourself how to get the data into R).
What was the most common month in which survey respondents were born?

🗂️ See Measure central tendency > Mode flash card.







TipHint





The variable that holds this information is the one called birthmonth. You can check what different variables are in your data by quickly using names(data), replacing “data” with whatever name you used to store your dataset in R.

Question 2


One of the questions in the survey asked about how spicy people liked their food.
The possible responses were:


Anti-spice: Mayonnaise is too spicy for me; I avoid any black pepper.
Mild: I like a tiny hint of warmth, but flavour comes first.
Medium: I enjoy a solid kick that makes the meal interesting.
Hot: I want to feel the burn.
Very Hot: I want to sweat and question my life choices.
Extreme: I want to transcend mortal existence and taste the fury of a thousand suns.


This has been recoded for you already so that the dataset contains both a variable with the descriptive word (“medium”, “hot” etc), and a variable with a numeric value (1 being assigned to “anti-spice” and 6 being assigned to “extreme”).
For what level of spicy-ness does half of the sample fall above and half fall below?

🗂️ See Measure central tendency > Median flash card.






Solution



Solution 2. 

sdata |> 
  summarise(
    spicy_Med = median(spicy_num, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# A tibble: 1 x 1

      <dbl>

title: W7: Z Scores & the Normal Distribution
text:
Pick someone new to be the driver this week. If everyone in the group has already had a week as the driver, start going round again!
The driver will type the code. The rest of you are navigators, you need to tell the driver where to go (i.e., what to type!).
Driver instructions:

Log in to the bigger screen at your table
Open RStudio Server
Open a new .R script, and load the tidyverse package.
Listen to your navigators

Navigator instructions:

Tell your driver where to go (i.e., what to type)!



Question 1


We’re continuing to use the same survey data for the remainder of the semester. The data are stored at https://uoepsy.github.io/data/dapr1_2526_survey.csv. By now, as a group you will have read in the data numerous times. Just check back to your work from the previous weeks to remind yourself if needs be.
This week we are working with the two questions about peoples outlook (pessimism/optimism) and their chronotype (evening/morning person).

These are on quite different scales (-100 to 100, and 0 to 10). Which means someone scoring 10 on outlook means a very different thing to them scoring 10 on ampm.
Task: Read in the data, and create two new variables, which are the standardised (or Z-) scores on these variables.

🗂️ TODO calc z score flashcard flash card.






Solution



Solution 1. 

library(tidyverse)
sdata <- read_csv("https://uoepsy.github.io/data/dapr1_2526_survey.csv")

sdata <- sdata |>
  mutate(
    outlookZ = ( outlook - mean(outlook) ) / sd(outlook),
    ampmZ = ( ampm - mean(ampm) ) / sd(ampm)
  )





Question 2


Find the pseudonyms, scores, and Z-scores of the three people who reported being the most optimistic, and the three who identified the most as “morning people”.






TipHint





One way to do this is to take the data (line 1 below), and then sort it by a variable, in descending order (line 2), before taking a “slice” of it and asking for specific row numbers (line 3). You can then, to make it easier to see stuff in the output, choose only the variables that you want to see (line 4):

data |>
  arrange(desc(variable)) |>
  slice(1:5) |>
  select(variable, variable2, variable3)


🗂️ TODO EP any flashcards potentially relevant? flash card.









Solution



Solution 2. 

sdata |> 
  arrange(desc(outlook)) |>
  slice(1:3) |>
  select(pseudonym, outlook, outlookZ)

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  pseudonym outlook outlookZ
  <chr>       <dbl>    <dbl>
1 <NA>          100     2.17
2 <NA>           93     1.91
3 <NA>           86     1.64

sdata |> 
  arrange(desc(ampm)) |>
  slice(1:3) |>
  select(pseudonym, ampm, ampmZ)

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  pseudonym   ampm ampmZ
  <chr>      <dbl> <dbl>
1 allscratch    10  1.55
2 <NA>          10  1.55
3 <NA>          10  1.55






Question 3


Plot the standardised outlook scores as a density curve.
Once you have made your plot, add this bit of code to the end of it. It will add a normal distribution (with mean of 0 and standard deviation of 1).

... 
  ... +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = 0, sd = 1), 
                colour = "red")


🗂️ See the Plot a variable > Histogram flash card. Only we don’t want a geom_histogram(), we want a geom_density()!






Solution



Solution 3. 

ggplot(sdata , aes(x = outlookZ)) +
  geom_density() +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = 0, sd = 1), colour = "red")












Question 4


In a “standard normal” distribution – a normal distribution with mean of 0 and sd of 1, often written \(N(0,1)\) – 90% of the distribution falls below 1.28. In other words, there is a 90% probability that a randomly drawn observation is < 1.28.















CautionRabbit hole: how to find this out for any %





In “the olden days” when everything was black and white, there were big tables of numbers that people had to look through to figure out this sort of thing.
Computers can do it in an instant. The qnorm() function in R takes a probability, and returns the value at which that area under the normal distribution falls.
Computers can do this in an instant. In R, the qnorm() function takes a probability and tells you the exact value where the area under the standard normal distribution curve reaches that amount.
E.g., 40% of the distribution falls to the left of:

qnorm(0.4)

[1] -0.253


And 50% of the distribution falls to the left of…
(we actually don’t need to calculate this - take a look above at the plot and think!)

qnorm(0.5)

[1] 0





Given this information, if we make the assumption for now that outlook is normally distributed, we should be able to figure out the value of the original outlook variable at which we would expect 90% of the distribution to fall.
Because we calculated the Z scores using \(z = \frac{x - M}{SD}\), we are essentially asking what value of \(x\) results in \(z = 1.28\). To do this we can rearrange \(Z = \frac{x - M}{SD}\) to \(x = (z \cdot SD) + M\), and then “plug in” the relevant numbers to calculate \(x\).
We’ll take this opportunity to introduce an alternative way to access variables in a dataframe. As well as calculating means and standard deviations using data |> summarise(), we can also get a specific variable using data$variable. This is easier for doing quick calculations such as:
The Z score for some hypothetical person who scored 20 on the optimism question:

(20 - mean(sdata$outlook)) / sd(sdata$outlook)

[1] -0.86


Task: calculate the value below which 90% of outlook scores fall.






TipHints





We’re wanting to calculate \(x\), using \(x = (z \cdot SD) + M\).
We know we want \(z = 1.28\), and we can use mean(sdata$outlook) and sd(sdata$outlook) for \(M\) and \(SD\) respectively.








Solution



Solution 4. 

(1.28*sd(sdata$outlook)) + mean(sdata$outlook)

[1] 76.4






Question 5


Find the outlook value for one of your group members. They will need to remember the pseudonym used to fill the survey.
We can extract a specific row with the filter() function, where we use two equals signs to ask “is a variable equal to <specific value>?”.
For example, to find any row where the pseudonym “dougal” was used:

sdata |> 
  filter(pseudonym == "dougal")

Assuming outlook is normally distributed, what is the probability of seeing somebody less optimistic than your chosen group member? And more optimistic?
Do the values satisfy the requirements of probabilities? Check that they are positive, less than 1, and they sum to 1






TipHints





See this week’s lecture slides - we’ll want to use pnorm()!
TODO I don’t know if we want a pnorm flashcard? do we have a link to the slides or are they only hosted on learn?








Solution



Solution 5. Dougal is a little bit of a pessimist:

sdata |> 
  filter(pseudonym == "dougal") |>
  select(pseudonym, outlook)

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  pseudonym outlook
  <chr>       <dbl>
1 dougal        -16


His outlook score of 16, when transformed to a Z-score, is:

dougalZ = (-16 - mean(sdata$outlook)) / sd(sdata$outlook)

There is a 1% probability of seeing someone less optimistic than Dougal, and a 99% probability of seeing someone more optimistic.

pnorm(dougalZ)

[1] 0.013

1-pnorm(dougalZ)

[1] 0.987






Finishing up
Once you’ve finished, don’t forget to:

Save your R script
Post the R script to the group discussion space on Learn, to ensure that everyone has access to it! (For step-by-step instructions on how to do this, click here)

title: W9: Confidence Intervals
text:
Pick someone new to be the driver this week. If everyone in the group has already had a week as the driver, start going round again!
The driver will type the code. The rest of you are navigators, you need to tell the driver where to go (i.e., what to type!).
Driver instructions:

Log in to the bigger screen at your table
Open RStudio Server
Open a new .R script, and load the tidyverse package.
Listen to your navigators

Navigator instructions:

Tell your driver where to go (i.e., what to type)!



Question 1


The code below gives us the means from lots and lots of samples. Last week we saw this used to get estimated means from 1000 samples, but this week we’ll up it to 10,000!

means100 <- replicate(10000, mean(rnorm(n = 100, mean = 35, sd = 20)))







Tipreminder/breakdown of how the code works





This bit of code takes a sample of size 100, from a distribution that has a mean of 35 and a standard deviation of 20.
It gives 100 numbers — in our example, each one of them is a persons’ “outlook” score.

rnorm(n = 100, mean = 35, sd = 20)

Wrapping the whole bit inside mean() makes it so that instead of returning all 100 scores in the sample, it returns just the mean of the 100 scores

mean( rnorm(n = 100, mean = 35, sd = 20) )

Finally, the function replicate() is used to “run code n times”. In this case, we’re running the mean(rnorm(...)) bit of code 10000 times. Each time, it takes a sample of 100 people’s scores and returns the estimated mean. So we get back 10000 means.

replicate(10000, mean( rnorm(n = 100, mean = 35, sd = 20) ) )

Finally, it stores those 10000 means in R using the name means100



Because means100 is a vector (it just has one dimension), if we want to find the 10th entry, we can use <vector name>[<entry-number>] to print it.
(Note, if you do this, you will get a different number, because you have a different set of 10000 samples!)

means100[10]

[1] 38.3


We also saw how we can create a dataframe object (with rows and columns), by using code such as the below. We’ve added a little extra bit here. Line 5 takes the dataframe created in lines 2-4, and arranges it (i.e. sorts it) according to the value in the estimate column. Which means the first row is now the smallest estimate, and the last row (row 10000) is the largest.

data100 <- 
  tibble(
    estimate = means100
  ) |> 
  arrange(estimate)

Task: What is the estimate for the 5000th row of the dataframe?
Bonus challenge: can we find this out another way?

🗂️ See TODO df[r,c] flashcard flash card.






Solution



Solution 1. Here is the 5000th row for me. Yours will be different, because each time we run the means100 <- replicate(10000, mean(rnorm...... bit of code, it takes a new 10000 random samples.

data100[5000, ]

# A tibble: 1 × 1
  estimate
     <dbl>
1     35.0


Because we have estimates from 10000 samples, ordered from smallest to largest, then the 5000th row is the one where 50% are above, and 50% are below - it’s the median!

data100 |>
  summarise(
    med_est = median(estimate)
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 1
  med_est
    <dbl>
1    35.0






Question 2


Create a new column of standardised (z-scored) estimates.

Look back to how we did this in week 7! See also…
🗂️ TODO z score calc flashcard flash card.






Solution



Solution 2. 

data100 <- 
  data100 |>
  mutate(
    est_Z = (estimate - mean(estimate)) / sd(estimate)
  )





Question 3


last week we saw two ways to quantify how much variability in an estimated mean we would expect due to sampling:

We could generate lots of samples of size \(n\), estimate their means, and calculate the standard deviation of all those estimated means
We could use the formula \(\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\), where \(\sigma\) is the standard deviation of scores in the population, and \(n\) is the size of the sample.

Both of these give us the “standard error”, or ‘how estimates from samples of size n vary around the population mean’. Another very useful way to express the precision in our estimate is to give the range between which 95% of the sample estimates will fall. This is known as a “confidence interval”.
We can, again, do this by either:

Generate lots of samples of size \(n\), estimate their means, and see where the middle 95% of the means fall
Use the formula \(\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\), along with the fact that 95% of a normal distribution falls within 1.96 SD of the mean.

We already have our “lots and lots of samples”, so let’s do 1 now.
Task: Because the data are already ordered by size of the estimate, and we have 10000 of them, we simply need to get the middle 9500 estimates. Extract two rows of the data, one that is the first row of the middle 9500, and one that is the last row of the middle 9500.. The value of estimate for these rows will give us the interval!
Bonus– what do you notice about the values of the z-scored/standardised column for these rows? They should be close to +/-1.96!






TipHint





if we have 10000 things, then the middle 9500 are between 250 and 9750!

🗂️ See TODO df[r,c] flashcard flash card.









Solution



Solution 3. 

data100[c(250,9750), ]

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  estimate est_Z
     <dbl> <dbl>
1     31.0 -2.01
2     38.8  1.95






Question 4


Let’s compare the interval we got in the previous question, to the one we get when we:

Use the formula \(\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\), along with the fact that 95% of a normal distribution falls within 1.96 SD of the mean.

We know that the mean is 35, and the standard deviation (\(\sigma\)) is 20. And we are taking samples of size \(n = 100\). All this means that we can calculate a confidence interval using:
\[
\begin{align}
\mu \pm 1.96 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} \\
\quad \\
35 \pm 1.96 \cdot \frac{20}{\sqrt{2}} \\
\end{align}
\]
Check that it matches the interval from the previous question (it might not be exact, but it should be very close!)






TipHint





This is just plugging in numbers and using R like a basic calculator.








Solution



Solution 4. 

35 - (1.96 * 20/sqrt(100))

[1] 31.1

35 + (1.96 * 20/sqrt(100))

[1] 38.9






Question 5


In all of what we have done this week and last week, we’ve been assuming that we already know the population mean and population standard deviation!!
When we have been generating samples, we knew to put 35 and 20 into the code rnorm(100, mean = .., sd = ..).
And when we have been using the formula, we have used those values in place of \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\).
But in reality, we don’t know anything about the population. That’s what we’re actually trying to learn about!
In real research, all we have is a single sample, and we have to go from there…
Our real sample is all of you!

sdata <- read_csv("https://uoepsy.github.io/data/dapr1_2526_survey.csv") |>
  select(pseudonym, outlook)

what do we do? well, we use our best guesses for \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\) - we use the mean (\(\bar x\)) and standard deviation (\(s\)) from our sample!
\[
\begin{align}
\bar x \pm 1.96 \cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} \\
\end{align}
\]
Task: calculate a confidence interval for the mean outlook score using the sample of 41 DAPR1 students.

🗂️ See flashcard flash card.







TipHint





We’ll need to replace parts of the calculation we used in the previous question. Instead of \(n=100\) we now have \(n = 41\), and we will also need to replace the numbers 35 and 20 with code to calculate sample estimate: mean(sdata$outlook) and sd(sdata$outlook)








Solution



Solution 5. 

mean(sdata$outlook) - (1.96 * sd(sdata$outlook)/sqrt(41))

[1] 34.6

mean(sdata$outlook) + (1.96 * sd(sdata$outlook)/sqrt(41))

[1] 50.8






Finishing up
Once you’ve finished, don’t forget to:

Save your R script
Post the R script to the group discussion space on Learn, to ensure that everyone has access to it! (For step-by-step instructions on how to do this, click here)

title: W11: One Sample T test
text:
Pick someone new to be the driver this week. If everyone in the group has already had a week as the driver, start going round again!
The driver will type the code. The rest of you are navigators, you need to tell the driver where to go (i.e., what to type!).
Driver instructions:

Log in to the bigger screen at your table
Open RStudio Server
Open a new .R script, and load the tidyverse package.
Listen to your navigators

Navigator instructions:

Tell your driver where to go (i.e., what to type)!


q1 t.test(sdata$outlook, mu=35, alternative=“greater”) q2 RQ “are DAPR1 students identify more as evening people or as morning people?” set up hypothesis q3 plot q4 t test q5 write up

Question 1


Our work last week culminated in performing our first null hypothesis test. We were testing whether the average optimism score in DAPR1 students is greater than the general population average (35).
To do this, we calculated a test statistic (Lines 6-9 below) and then computed the p-value (Line 11), to quantify the probability of observing a test-statistic at least as extreme as the one we have got.

# packages:
library(tidyverse)
# data:
sdata <- read_csv("https://uoepsy.github.io/data/dapr1_2526_survey.csv")

# standard error of mean:
se <- sd(sdata$outlook) / sqrt(nrow(sdata))
# test statistic:  
zstat <- (mean(sdata$outlook) - 35) / se
# p-value
1-pnorm(zstat)

[1] 0.0311


Good news everyone! There’s a function in R that does this test for us! It’s the t.test() function.
Note… it’s \(t\), and not \(Z\). That’s because when we have been calculating the standard error, we have been using our sample standard deviation, sd(sdata$outlook), rather than the population standard deviation \(\sigma\). That’s because we don’t know what \(\sigma\) is.
When we use the sample standard deviation, we’re using an estimate of \(\sigma\), which means we are introducing more uncertainty. This uncertainty depends on how big our sample is.
Our test statistic \(\frac{M-35}{s/\sqrt{n}}\), when we use \(s\) not \(\sigma\), is actually a \(t\)-statistic. It doesn’t follow a normal distribution, it follows a \(t\)-distribution.
\(t\)-distributions look very like the normal distribution, but the tails get thicker as the “degrees of freedom” decrease. The “degrees of freedom” here are \(n-1\), because we have \(n\) observations and need to use 1 estimate (the mean) to calculate \(s\).
Task: Use t.test() to perform the same hypothesis test but as a \(t\)-test, not \(z\).
